name: Saint-Domingue
title: Social Hierarchy of Saint-Domingue: From Governor to Enslaved
period: c. 1750–1789 (the French colony at its richest, before the Haitian Revolution)

tiers.name: The governor-general and the intendant
tiers.you: You govern the king’s richest colony for a few years at most, command its troops and militia, and enforce trade rules that the planters around you resent.
tiers.kid: A governor and an intendant sent from France ran Saint-Domingue for the king.
tiers.rise: The king appointed both officials, the governor usually from the nobility and the officers of the army or navy, the intendant from the royal administration; few stayed more than a few years before recall, promotion or death.
tiers.why: Saint-Domingue, the richest colony of the French crown, was governed for the king by two officials sent from France.

tiers.name: Great planters and merchants
tiers.you: You own a sugar estate worked by hundreds of enslaved people, which you may run from France through a manager, and you resent the trade rules made in Versailles.
tiers.kid: The richest white planters owned huge sugar farms, and many of them lived far away in France.
tiers.rise: Wealth made a grand blanc: a fortune in sugar, trade or office, often built by an earlier generation or gained by marrying into a planter family. Debt, epidemics or a fall in prices could ruin an estate: the collapse of coffee profits around 1770 drove many planters into debt.
tiers.why: At the top of colonial society stood the grands blancs, the “big whites”: the owners of the great sugar estates, the leading merchants of Cap-Français and Port-au-Prince, and the senior officials and officers.

tiers.name: Poorer whites
tiers.you: You came from France to make your fortune as an overseer, artisan or shopkeeper; you may own a few enslaved people, and the colony’s law ranks you above every person of colour, however rich.
tiers.kid: Poorer white people worked as overseers, craftsmen and shopkeepers, and many of them died of fevers.
tiers.rise: A petit blanc could rise by managing an absentee’s estate, by trade or by marriage, and buy land and enslaved workers of his own; a lucky few joined the grands blancs, while many died young of disease.
tiers.why: Most whites were petits blancs, “little whites”: overseers and managers on the plantations, artisans, shopkeepers, clerks, sailors, soldiers, slave dealers and day labourers, along with small planters of coffee, indigo…

tiers.name: Free people of colour
tiers.you: You were born free, perhaps the child of a planter, and may own land, a trade and even enslaved workers of your own, yet the law bars you from office, the respected professions and the dress and weapons of whites.
tiers.kid: Free people of colour could own farms and businesses, but unfair laws kept them out of many jobs.
tiers.rise: Freedom came through manumission, which needed official permission and a tax, through purchase, or by birth to a free mother; a few families, after generations of marriage with whites, came to count as white. From the 1760s the laws closed most other doors.
tiers.why: Saint-Domingue had the largest and richest free population of colour in the Caribbean.

tiers.name: Enslaved drivers, craftsmen and house servants
tiers.you: You were born in the colony and drive a field gang, boil the sugar or serve in the great house; you eat better and move more freely than the field hands, but you are still property and can be sent back to the fields.
tiers.kid: Some enslaved people were skilled craftsmen, drivers or house servants, but they were still owned by others.
tiers.rise: Owners promoted trusted or skilled workers, most often creoles, and could demote them at will; such people were the enslaved most likely to be freed, as the coachman Toussaint Louverture was in the 1770s.
tiers.why: The plantations kept a hierarchy of their own among the enslaved.

tiers.name: Enslaved field workers
tiers.term: esclaves de jardin; bossales (born in Africa)
tiers.you: You were probably born in Africa and carried across the Atlantic; you cut cane or work coffee under a driver’s whip, grow food on a garden plot, and can be sold at your owner’s will.
tiers.kid: Most people in Saint-Domingue were enslaved and forced to work on sugar and coffee farms without pay.
tiers.rise: Freedom came rarely, by an owner’s grant, which needed official permission and a tax, or by purchase, which many owners refused; others fled. A child took its mother’s status (article 13 of the Code Noir), so the children of enslaved women were born enslaved.
tiers.why: The great majority of Saint-Domingue’s people were enslaved field workers, and about two-thirds of them had been born in Africa.

tiers.name: Maroons
tiers.you: You have fled your owner for the mountains, where you farm, hunt and raid plantations with a maroon band; if the rural police catch you, the law prescribes mutilation, and death for a third flight.
tiers.kid: Maroons were people who escaped from slavery and made free homes for themselves in the mountains.
tiers.rise: Flight was the only way in; capture, surrender or a treaty such as Santiago’s were the ways out.
